intro: All four translate as 'if' or 'when', but each looks at the link between A and B from a different angle. と is a mechanism: whenever A happens, B follows by itself. ば puts the weight on the condition: B holds provided A holds. たら is a time line: once A has actually happened, then B. なら takes A as given (often something just said) and comments on it: if that is the case, then B. Choose by asking what kind of link you mean, and check what may stand at the end of the sentence.

skills.rule: A と B: every time A happens, B follows automatically, so B is never a request, wish, plan or invitation.
skills.explain:
と joins A to an outcome that comes with it without anyone deciding: laws of nature (春になると桜が咲く), how machines work (押すとお湯が出る), directions (右に曲がると駅がある), and a person's fixed habits. It attaches to the plain non-past form: 行くと, 高いと, 静かだと, 学生だと.

In the past, A と B(た) reports what you found or what happened next: 窓を開けると海が見えた ('when I opened the window, there was the sea'). In narration it can also carry one person's next action: 家に帰ると、すぐ宿題をした.

The hard edge: the main clause cannot express the speaker's will. 〜てください, 〜ましょう, 〜たい, 〜つもり and 〜ほうがいい after と are wrong; use たら (one-off event) or なら (advice). と also cannot look forward to a single hoped-for event.

examples.jp: 春[はる]になる{と}、桜[さくら]が咲[さ]きます。
examples.en: When spring comes, the cherry trees blossom.

examples.jp: このボタンを押[お]す{と}、お湯[ゆ]が出[で]ます。
examples.en: If you press this button, hot water comes out.

examples.jp: 二[ふた]つ目[め]の角[かど]を右[みぎ]に曲[ま]がる{と}、駅[えき]が見[み]えます。
examples.en: Turn right at the second corner and you will see the station.

examples.jp: 祖父[そふ]は朝[あさ]起[お]きる{と}、まず散歩[さんぽ]に行[い]きます。
examples.en: The first thing my grandfather does after getting up is go for a walk.

examples.jp: 窓[まど]を開[あ]ける{と}、海[うみ]が見[み]えた。
examples.en: When I opened the window, I could see the sea.

contrast.note: たら is for a single event that may or may not happen, and allows a request after it: 駅に着いたら電話して. と is for what always happens: 駅に着くと、いつも母に電話する.
ば also states general conditions, but stresses that A is the requirement (安ければ買う: only if cheap). と stresses that B simply follows (安いと売れる: cheap things sell).

mistakes.bad: 駅[えき]に着[つ]く{と}、電話[でんわ]してください。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]に着[つ]い{たら}、電話[でんわ]してください。
mistakes.note: A request cannot follow と; a one-off 'once you arrive' takes たら.

mistakes.bad: 夏休[なつやす]みになる{と}、北海道[ほっかいどう]へ行[い]きたいです。
mistakes.good: 夏休[なつやす]みになっ{たら}、北海道[ほっかいどう]へ行[い]きたいです。
mistakes.note: A wish is the speaker's will, which と cannot introduce.

skills.tip: Could you add 'always' or 'automatically' to B? Then と. Is B a request, wish or plan? Then never と.

skills.rule: A ば B: B holds on condition that A holds; it is the 'provided that' conditional, and the form behind 〜ばいい and 〜ば〜ほど.
skills.explain:
ば puts the spotlight on the condition itself: if A is met, B follows (安ければ買う 'I'll buy it if it's cheap', and by implication not otherwise). Formation: godan 行く→行けば, ichidan 見る→見れば, する→すれば, 来る→くれば, い-adjective 高い→高ければ, negative ない→なければ. Nouns and な-adjectives use なら(ば).

If A is an action verb, B cannot be a request, invitation or intention: say 着いたら電話して, not 着けば. If A is a state (ある, いる, できる, an adjective, a negative), a request is fine: 時間があれば手伝ってください.

Fixed uses: どうすればいいですか 'what should I do?', 〜ばいい 'you only need to', 〜ば〜ほど 'the more ..., the more ...', and 〜ばよかった 'I wish I had'. ば does not report a single real past event: use たら or と for that.
patterns: どう すれば いいですか / [verb]ば いいです

examples.jp: 安[やす]けれ{ば}、買[か]います。
examples.en: If it's cheap, I'll buy it.

examples.jp: 時間[じかん]があれ{ば}、手伝[てつだ]ってください。
examples.en: If you have time, please give me a hand.

examples.jp: この薬[くすり]を飲[の]め{ば}、すぐ治[なお]りますよ。
examples.en: If you take this medicine, you'll get better quickly.

examples.jp: 切符[きっぷ]はどこで買[か]え{ば}いいですか。
examples.en: Where should I buy a ticket?

examples.jp: 練習[れんしゅう]すれ{ば}するほど、上手[じょうず]になります。
examples.en: The more you practise, the better you get.

examples.jp: もっと早[はや]く家[いえ]を出[で]れ{ば}よかった。
examples.en: I should have left home earlier.

contrast.note: Both cover hypotheticals, but たら follows a one-off event in time and accepts any ending: 東京に着いたら連絡します. 着けば連絡します is wrong, because an action verb with ば cannot lead to the speaker's own plan.
と reports an automatic result; ば makes A a requirement. 〜ば〜ほど is fixed to ば; in 'what should I do?' ば and たら both work (どうすればいい / どうしたらいい), but と does not.
なら takes A as given and advises; ば states what A brings about. 京都へ行くなら秋がいい (advice for a trip you are planning), not 行けば.

mistakes.bad: 駅[えき]に着[つ]け{ば}、電話[でんわ]してください。
mistakes.good: 駅[えき]に着[つ]い{たら}、電話[でんわ]してください。
mistakes.note: After an action verb with ば the main clause cannot be a request; use たら.

mistakes.bad: 昨日[きのう]家[いえ]に帰[かえ]れ{ば}、荷物[にもつ]が届[とど]いていた。
mistakes.good: 昨日[きのう]家[いえ]に帰[かえ]っ{たら}、荷物[にもつ]が届[とど]いていた。
mistakes.note: ば does not narrate a real past event; a discovery takes たら or と.

skills.tip: Can you say 'provided that', 'only if', 'should I' or 'the more'? Then ば. Action verb plus a request after it? Switch to たら.

skills.rule: A たら B: once A has happened, B; the all-purpose conditional for single events, also used for discoveries and for suggestions with 〜たらどう.
skills.explain:
たら is the past form plus ら: 行ったら, 読んだら, 高かったら, 静かだったら, 雨だったら. It means A is completed first and B comes after it. That makes it the natural choice for one-off future events, certain ('once', 'when') or uncertain ('if'): 二十歳になったら, 雨が降ったら. Any ending may follow: requests, invitations, wishes, plans.

With a past B it reports what you found or what happened to you: 箱を開けたら空だった. It does not narrate your own next deliberate action: not 家に帰ったら宿題をした, but 帰ると or 帰ってから. 〜たらどう(ですか) is a friendly suggestion ('why don't you ...?').

Its limit is order in time: A must happen before B. If B has to be done before A, as with advice for a trip, use なら.

examples.jp: 雨[あめ]が降[ふ]っ{たら}、試合[しあい]は中止[ちゅうし]です。
examples.en: If it rains, the match will be called off.

examples.jp: 家[いえ]に着[つ]い{たら}、連絡[れんらく]してね。
examples.en: Let me know once you get home.

examples.jp: 二十歳[はたち]になっ{たら}、お酒[さけ]が飲[の]めます。
examples.en: Once you turn twenty, you can drink alcohol.

examples.jp: 箱[はこ]を開[あ]け{たら}、中[なか]は空[から]だった。
examples.en: When I opened the box, it was empty.

examples.jp: 一度[いちど]医者[いしゃ]に診[み]てもらっ{たら}どうですか。
examples.en: Why don't you get a doctor to look at it?

contrast.note: たら: A first, then B. なら: given that A is the plan, B (even before A). 中国へ行ったら、ビザを取って is wrong; 中国へ行くなら、ビザを取って is right.
と suits fixed, repeated results and cannot take a request; たら suits one event and takes anything. For a discovery in the past both work: 開けたら / 開けると、空だった.
After an action verb ば cannot take a request; たら can. 〜ば〜ほど takes only ば; for a friendly suggestion use 〜たらどう. 〜たらいい and 〜ばいい ('what should I do?') are both standard.

mistakes.bad: 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ行[い]っ{たら}、暖[あたた]かいコートを買[か]っておいたほうがいいですよ。
mistakes.good: 北海道[ほっかいどう]へ行[い]く{なら}、暖[あたた]かいコートを買[か]っておいたほうがいいですよ。
mistakes.note: The coat is bought before the trip, so B comes first in time: なら.

mistakes.bad: 家[いえ]に帰[かえ]っ{たら}、すぐ宿題[しゅくだい]をした。
mistakes.good: 家[いえ]に帰[かえ]る{と}、すぐ宿題[しゅくだい]をした。
mistakes.note: In the past, たら reports what you found or what befell you, not your own next action.

skills.tip: Picture a timeline: A done, then B. If that fits and it is a single event, たら is safe with any ending.

skills.rule: A なら B: if A is the case (as you say, or as I assume), then here is B; used to take up a topic or plan and give advice about it.
skills.explain:
なら does not describe a chain of events. It accepts A as a premise, usually something the listener has just said or plainly intends, and the speaker answers with advice, an opinion or a decision. It attaches to the plain form of verbs and adjectives (行くなら, 行ったなら, 高いなら) and directly to nouns and な-adjectives (学生なら, 静かなら).

Because A is only a premise, B may come before A in time: 京都へ行くなら、早めにホテルを予約したほうがいい. With a noun it means 'if it's X you want, speaking of X': 寿司なら、あの店.

The limits: なら cannot state natural or automatic consequences (春になると, not なるなら), cannot report a past discovery, and does not mean 'once A is over' (着いたら連絡して, not 着くなら).

examples.jp: 寿司[すし]{なら}、駅前[えきまえ]の店[みせ]がおいしいですよ。
examples.en: If it's sushi you want, the place in front of the station is good.

examples.jp: 眠[ねむ]い{なら}、先[さき]に寝[ね]ていいよ。
examples.en: If you're sleepy, go ahead and go to bed.

examples.jp: 京都[きょうと]へ行[い]く{なら}、秋[あき]がいいですよ。
examples.en: If you're going to Kyoto, autumn is the time to go.

examples.jp: パソコンを買[か]う{なら}、軽[かる]いのがいいと思[おも]います。
examples.en: If you're buying a computer, I'd go for a light one.

examples.jp: 田中[たなか]さんが行[い]かない{なら}、私[わたし]も行[い]きません。
examples.en: If Mr Tanaka isn't going, I'm not going either.

contrast.note: たら needs A to happen first. 日本に来たら連絡して: contact me after you arrive. 日本に来るなら連絡して: if you're planning to come, tell me (beforehand).
と states what always follows; なら gives a view on a particular premise. 春になると暖かくなる, never 春になるなら.
With nouns and な-adjectives the ば form is itself なら(ば), but for verbs ば is a condition with a result, not advice on a premise.

mistakes.bad: 春[はる]になる{なら}、桜[さくら]が咲[さ]きます。
mistakes.good: 春[はる]になる{と}、桜[さくら]が咲[さ]きます。
mistakes.note: A natural, automatic consequence takes と, not なら.

mistakes.bad: 窓[まど]を開[あ]ける{なら}、富士山[ふじさん]が見[み]えた。
mistakes.good: 窓[まど]を開[あ]け{たら}、富士山[ふじさん]が見[み]えた。
mistakes.note: なら cannot report something you found in the past.

skills.tip: Can you say 'if that's the case' or 'if it's X you're after'? Then なら. If B must happen before A, なら is the only choice.
